section_summary: This section follows negotiations over Japan’s Petroleum Industry Law and its requirement that oil companies hold six months’ stocks. American and British companies resisted the cost and uncertainty, offered a coal hydrogenation process, and then discussed possible guarantees for trade, prices, storage limits, and refining rights. Embassy reports and their enclosures record Japan’s initial enforcement warning and a subsequent, more conciliatory search for an agreement.

people.name: Stanley K. Hornbeck
people.role: Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

people.name: Saburō Kurusu
people.role: Chief of the Japanese Foreign Office’s Bureau of Commercial Affairs

people.name: Shinji Yoshino
people.role: Japanese Vice Minister for Commerce and Industry

people.name: Machida
people.role: Japanese Minister for Commerce and Industry

people.name: Shigemitsu
people.role: Japanese Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs

subfiles.title: Parker to Hornbeck enclosing Yokohama cable
subfiles.from: P. W. Parker, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: Forwards a Yokohama report on renewed discussions with Kurusu.
subfiles.summary: Parker sends a cable summarizing talks on Japan’s oil-control law.

subfiles.title: Yokohama report on talks with Kurusu
subfiles.about: Reports Kurusu’s suggestions for guarantees or Japanese participation in oil distribution.
subfiles.summary: Despite severe OCR loss, the cable records proposals for guaranteed trading volume, remunerative prices, a maximum storage obligation, and use of Japanese capital for stocks and distribution.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck’s acknowledgment to Parker
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Parker’s letter and Yokohama cable.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck expects to hear Standard-Vacuum’s decisions on the matter.

subfiles.title: Division note on Tokyo despatch 1609
subfiles.about: Summarizes prior telegrams and the Ambassador’s January 7 approach.
subfiles.summary: Notes that telegrams covered the despatch and Shigemitsu promised reasonable economic returns.

subfiles.title: American oil interests in Japan, despatch 1609
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the companies’ refusal of six-month stocks and ensuing diplomatic discussions.
subfiles.summary: Standard-Vacuum and Rising Sun rejected the storage requirement and offered a coal hydrogenation license in exchange for the Five Point program. Kurusu discussed withdrawal, reduced quotas, guarantees, and Japanese distribution partners. The British Ambassador raised the issue informally, while Grew planned a similar approach.

subfiles.title: Oil companies’ letter to Yoshino
subfiles.from: Rising Sun Petroleum Company and Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: Rejects added storage investment and proposes a coal hydrogenation license.
subfiles.summary: The companies argue that annual quotas, requisition prices, and replenishment duties make six-month storage commercially untenable. They offer hydrogenation patents and expertise as a means of securing Japan’s emergency oil supply.

subfiles.title: Dickover’s conversation with Kurusu
subfiles.about: Records Kurusu’s proposed alternatives for foreign oil companies.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu suggested withdrawal, guaranteed trade with six-month storage, reduced quotas, or Japanese capital taking over distribution and stocks. Dickover raised doubts about profits, prices, and surrendering established businesses. Kurusu dismissed the hydrogenation exchange as costly and unnecessary.

subfiles.title: Japanese verbal notice on petroleum stock obligations
subfiles.about: Warns that Japan will enforce its six-month oil-stock requirement.
subfiles.summary: The notice says the Five Point talks do not bind the government. It threatens legal sanctions and quota reductions for noncompliance and treats coal liquefaction as a separate issue.

subfiles.title: Instruction to London forwarding despatch 1609
subfiles.about: Forwards Tokyo despatch 1609 and its enclosures.
subfiles.summary: Sends the London embassy the latest report on Japan’s oil situation.

subfiles.title: Division note on Tokyo telegram 12
subfiles.about: Assigns consideration of Japan’s proposal to the companies’ head offices.
subfiles.summary: Records that New York and London must decide; State needs no immediate action.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram 12 on proposed guarantees
subfiles.about: Reports Japan’s willingness to consider guarantees for oil-company compliance.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu says Yoshino agrees in principle to guarantees on quotas, profits, maximum stocks, and equal refining treatment. He asks the companies for terms; the embassy recommends careful consideration.

subfiles.title: Thompson’s conversation at the State Department
subfiles.about: Records disagreements among oil interests and confidential British assessments.
subfiles.summary: Thompson describes a split over Japanese partnership and storage, with a decision likely delayed. He also passes on a Shell report about British views of Japan’s foreign relations, which those present regard skeptically.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Tokyo forwarding Thompson memorandum
subfiles.about: Forwards the January 9 Thompson conversation memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Provides Tokyo with Thompson’s account of oil-company deliberations.

subfiles.title: Division note on Tokyo despatch 1629
subfiles.about: Summarizes the despatch and later telegram on potential oil guarantees.
subfiles.summary: The note says the January 15 telegram superseded much of the despatch’s detail.

subfiles.title: American oil interests in Japan, despatch 1629
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports company and diplomatic conversations about possible settlement terms.
subfiles.summary: The oil companies differed over whether to hold out for the Five Point program or explore guarantees while retaining their refusal of six-month stocks. Kurusu and Dickover discussed storage, Japanese partnerships, refining, and secure trade. Grew raised the companies’ position with Shigemitsu, who said Japan did not intend to deny them a reasonable return.

subfiles.title: Notes of December 27 meeting with Kurusu
subfiles.about: Records Kurusu’s alternatives and the companies’ objections.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu proposed reduced trade, Japanese distributors, or guarantees covering trade, prices, and a storage ceiling. Ely and Meyer defended the hydrogenation offer and pressed for secure terms, while resisting transfer of their distribution businesses.

subfiles.title: Dickover’s January 8 conversation with Kurusu
subfiles.about: Explores guarantees, storage, partnerships, and refining with Kurusu.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu considered guarantees for quotas, duration, and prices but saw little prospect of changing the law. Dickover explained the companies’ objections to investment and Japanese control of distribution. Kurusu concluded that guaranteed profitable business might provide a compromise.

subfiles.title: Instruction to London forwarding oil papers
subfiles.about: Forwards Thompson’s memorandum and Tokyo despatch 1629.
subfiles.summary: Supplies London with recent records of the Japan oil negotiations.

subfiles.title: Trade ‘Open Door’ Pledged in Manchukuo
subfiles.from: Sterling Fisher Jr., New York Times
subfiles.about: Reports Minami’s pledge to respect foreign business interests in Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The article links the pledge to criticism of Manchukuo’s oil monopoly.

subfiles.title: Division note on Tokyo despatch 1653
subfiles.about: Summarizes conciliatory talks and possible terms for oil-stock compliance.
subfiles.summary: Japan appears willing to discuss compensation, fixed stocks, and guarantees for trade volume, duration, and prices. The note records the companies’ concern that other countries might copy the storage law and recommends no immediate State Department action.

subfiles.title: American oil interests in Japan, despatch 1653
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports progress toward a negotiated arrangement under the Petroleum Industry Law.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu says Yoshino will consider guarantees on quotas, trading period, prices, and equal refining treatment. The companies prepare proposals but fear that Japan’s storage rule will spread abroad and become impossible to meet. Grew sees a more conciliatory Japanese stance and a possible fixed stock quantity alongside trade guarantees.

subfiles.title: Notes of January 11 interview with Kurusu
subfiles.about: Records Yoshino’s agreement in principle to consider guarantees.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu asks Ely and Meyer for concrete terms on trade, prices, storage, and refining. He says Japanese partnership is optional and requests a prompt proposal before later quotas are set.

subfiles.title: New York cable to Yokohama on proposed terms
subfiles.about: Requests discussion of the global precedent set by Japan’s storage law.
subfiles.summary: New York is preparing proposals and expects guarantees on quotas, prices, trading duration, and nondiscrimination. It says wider adoption of compulsory stocks could become physically impossible for the industry.

subfiles.title: Notes of January 18 interview with Kurusu
subfiles.about: Raises the risk that other countries will copy Japan’s storage requirement.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu understands the concern and arranges to discuss it with Yoshino.
